title: The Zahiris
hook: the literalist school of Ibn Hazm, now small

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ibadis, and your line: the ibadis of oman. Did you get to call someone by the name they'd choose for themselves? Day one thousand two hundred five.

A sign on a park gate says: no dogs. Someone walks in with a pet wolf. Is that allowed? One kind of reader reaches for the purpose behind the sign and says no, obviously. But there's another kind of reader, who stops and asks: who decides what the sign meant beyond what it says? If the rule-maker wanted wolves kept out, couldn't the rule-maker have written it? That second reader isn't being silly. That reader is protecting the text from everyone's guesses. In Islamic law, that reader had a school. Its great voice lived in Muslim Spain. Today, the Zahiris.
screen: `NO DOGS. IN COMES A WOLF.` → `THE PURPOSE, OR THE WORDS?` → `A SCHOOL OF THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Zahir is Arabic for what's outward, what shows on the surface. The Zahiris are the people of the plain sense: the law is what the Qur'an and the sunnah actually say, read in their apparent meaning. Tradition names Dawud al-Zahiri of Baghdad as the school's founder. Next, the tool they put down. Other schools use qiyas, analogy: if wine is forbidden because it intoxicates, then so is any drink that intoxicates. The Zahiris refused analogy as a source of law. Where the texts speak, follow them. Where they're silent, the matter is left open, and no jurist may close it with a guess. Then, their great voice. Ibn Hazm of Cordoba took the school's method and wrote it out at full length, in a book of law called al-Muhalla, arguing case by case. Tradition remembers him as sharp-tongued and fearless in debate, and he also wrote a book about love, The Ring of the Dove, full of lovers, glances and letters. Last, a test case. The Qur'an tells children, about aging parents, in Pickthall's words, "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word." An analogist says: if even 'fie' is forbidden, then striking a parent is forbidden all the more. A Zahiri agrees on the result, but not the route. The same verses already command kindness and gracious words, and other texts forbid harm. The plain sense is enough. The school is small today, but its question still sits in classrooms of fiqh: are you reading the text, or reading yourself into it?
screen: `ZAHIR: WHAT SHOWS ON THE SURFACE.` · `NO ANALOGY. SILENCE STAYS OPEN.` · `IBN HAZM OF CORDOBA.` · `NOT EVEN 'FIE.'`

segments.voice: The practice: read a text literally, then in context. Pick one short message you got recently, a text, an email, a note on the fridge. Read it once exactly as written, nothing added. What does it actually say? Now read it again with everything you know about the person who sent it. What do you think they meant? Notice the gap between the two readings, and how much of the second one you supplied yourself. If you pray, you can ask to read well. The bell holds the time.
The Zahiris. The school of the plain sense: the law is what the texts outwardly say, with no analogy to fill their silences. Today's word.

Your line: the plain sense. Today, before you decide what someone meant, read what they actually said one more time. Tomorrow, a message from Jordan about all these schools at once. Day one thousand two hundred five.

howItsDone: Zahiri jurists derive law only from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and sunnah, rejecting analogy (qiyas); the school is small today, but Ibn Hazm's books are still read by students of law.

fork.reveal: for the Zahiris, silence in the texts leaves a matter open. a jurist's comparison can't add a rule the texts didn't make.

original.note: Arabic: the Zahiris, from zahir, outward, apparent.

trapdoor: what you thought: literalists just read the words and stop thinking.
what it means: the Zahiris read the plain sense on purpose, to keep jurists' guesses from becoming law.
what a scholar hears: Dawud al-Zahiri, Ibn Hazm's al-Muhalla, the rejection of qiyas, and Tawq al-Hamama, The Ring of the Dove.
